claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by dislocation accumulation and dynamic recovery at nanoscale layer interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion and compositional complexity inhibit homogeneous dislocation glide in these multilayers.
Impeded dislocations pile up at FCC/BCC interfaces and produce local stress concentrations.
Interfacial stress concentrations eventually relax through dislocation climb or local interface decohesion.
The proposed starting coating has alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with sharp, coherent interfaces and uniform nanoscale layer thickness.
The proposed starting coating has a low initial dislocation density.
Sustained applied stress generates dislocations within the high-entropy-alloy layers.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order impede the generated dislocations.
Dynamic recovery by dislocation climb permits gradual plastic strain under sustained loading.
Whether interfaces remain effective dislocation barriers or decohere depends on individual layer thickness.
Sustained loading will produce a measurable time-dependent increase in plastic strain relative to the initial state.
Creep will be more pronounced in multilayers with thicker individual layers or less robust interfaces.
Thinner layers will improve interface-mediated dislocation interactions and reduce the creep rate.
The as-deposited baseline will show minimal early plastic deformation under comparable testing conditions.
Near 0.4 of the melting temperature, dislocation-based plasticity rather than grain-boundary diffusion is expected to dominate.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply at extreme temperatures or after degradation of the multilayer structure.
Systematically changing layer thickness or interface coherency should produce corresponding differences in creep rate and interfacial dislocation structures if the proposed mechanism is controlling.
